title: HSBC, J.P. Morgan and StoneX complete first live trades using Pooled Gold Interests (PGI) - Kitco
content: Kitco NEWS has a diverse team of journalists reporting on the economy, stock markets, commodities, cryptocurrencies, mining and metals with accuracy and objectivity. Our goal is to help people make informed market decisions through in-depth reporting, daily market roundups, interviews with prominent industry figures, comprehensive coverage (often exclusive) of important industry events and analyses of market-affecting developments. (Kitco News) – Gold’s digital evolution passed a major milestone on Tuesday after HSBC, J.P. Morgan and StoneX conducted wholesale-market transactions using Pooled Gold Interests (PGI) for the first time. PGI is the underpinning of the World Gold Council’s Wholesale Digital Gold initiative, and Tuesday’s pilot transactions represent a significant step towards a new way for institutions to own, transfer and use gold. “Loco London physical 400-ounce Good Delivery gold bars were placed into the Wholesale Digital Gold ecosystem, and PGI were created, giving participants proprietary interests over pooled gold,” the WGC said in its announcement. “Once the transactions were settled, the gold was withdrawn from the ecosystem, completing the full lifecycle.” ICE Benchmark Administration (IBA) acted as the operator for the transactions, and Baton Systems was the technology provider. “Today, Wholesale Digital Gold moved from concept to reality,” said David Tait, Chief Executive Officer of the World Gold Council. “For the first time, leading institutions have transferred, settled and used fractional ownership of physical gold as collateral through real, live transactions. This is a historic step forward for the gold market, preserving trust in physical ownership while opening up new ways for gold to be used in modern financial markets.” “J.P. Morgan is one of the largest and most active participants in the global precious metals market, with a presence that spans trading, clearing, vaulting and financing across every major hub,” said Mark Amlin, Global Head of Physical Commodities at J.P. Morgan. “That global footprint gives us a clear view of where the market’s infrastructure needs to evolve. Gold ownership that is fractional, readily transferable and insolvency remote would allow gold to be used more widely across financial markets, including as collateral.” Richard Anthony, Global Head of Macro eRisk and Precious Metals at HSBC, noted that the London-based bank has been participating in the precious metals market for more than 160 years since its founding in Hong Kong, and remains one of the world’s largest gold custodians and clearers. “We continue to invest in technology, including our gold tokenisation capabilities, to enable our clients to have greater access to gold,” Anthony said. “Developing a modern digital infrastructure for gold ownership and settlement is important to the overall market.” Michael Skinner, Global Head of Metals at StoneX, said the firm was pleased to have been involved in the Wholesale Digital Gold initiative from the outset. “StoneX has invested consistently in developing new solutions across commodities markets, from vaulting and refining through to execution and clearing, and we support initiatives like this one because they have the potential to deliver materially better outcomes for our clients — greater flexibility, lower operational friction and more efficient use of capital,” he said. The Wholesale Digital Gold initiative aims to address a longstanding challenge for the industry: how to preserve the integrity and trust of physical gold ownership while making gold easier to trade and use across modern financial markets. The WGC said this pilot demonstrates how digitalization can help gold move more efficiently through financial markets. The initiative was first launched in September 2025 in the white paper Pooled Gold Interests and Wholesale Digital Gold – A New Vision for the Gold Market. Morgan Asset Management has released its 2027 Long-Term Capital Market Assumptions, projecting a 7.1% annual return for a balanced AUD 60/40 portfolio over the next 10 to 15 years, marking one of the most constructive long-term outlooks the firm has published in over a decade. The 31st edition of the widely watched report released this week reflects a fundamental reassessment of global growth potential driven by artificial intelligence adoption, a generational reset in bond yields, and a structural shift in how capital flows across the world economy. While the LTCMAs are a long-term strategic planning tool rather than a short-term trading signal, the report carries significant weight across institutional portfolio management desks globally. The projections represent a meaningful upward revision from prior years, with the U.S. large cap equity forecast jumping 170 basis points to 7.9% and the global aggregate bond return forecast reaching 5.7%, its highest level in two decades. For context, the global aggregate bond projection sat at just 2.2% in 2021, underscoring the scale of the reset that has taken place in fixed income markets since the post-pandemic rate cycle began. Australian shares are projected to return 7.2%, up 20 basis points from the 2026 edition. The report arrives at a moment when markets are grappling with elevated inflation uncertainty, geopolitical fragmentation, and the uneven distribution of technology-driven productivity gains. The LTCMAs provide a structured, data-driven framework against which institutional allocators, superannuation funds, and wealth managers benchmark their strategic asset allocation decisions. J.P. Morgan’s research team identifies three structural forces underpinning the updated return assumptions. The first is economic nationalism, which is boosting domestic capital investment through reshoring and industrial policy but simultaneously creating crosscurrents of inflation volatility. The second is technology adoption, with AI investment expected to drive a $15 trillion global capital expenditure surge through to 2040. The third is capital rewiring, as public and private capital flows are redirected by shifting geopolitical alliances and supply chain restructuring. The cumulative effect of these forces is the best developed world growth outlook the report has projected in 15 years. Total factor productivity is forecast to increase by 50%, reaching 120 basis points, pushing U.S. real GDP growth expectations to 2.1% and developed world nominal GDP growth to 4.2%. Critically, J.P. Morgan describes the current mix of GDP growth relative to inflation as the most favorable since the pandemic, a signal that the earnings environment for corporates remains broadly supportive. U.S. large cap equities are the standout upgrade in the equity space. Corporate profit margins above 15% and the structural advantage the U.S. holds in AI infrastructure deployment are cited as the primary drivers behind the 170 basis point increase in the return forecast to 7.9%. In a notable historical first for the 31-year-old publication, developed market equity return projections have now overtaken those of emerging markets. Global equities are also projected at 7.9%, while emerging markets trail at 7.5%, reflecting the concentration of early-stage AI capital expenditure benefits in developed economies. On the fixed income side, U.S. Treasuries are expected to return 5.1%, supported by higher cash rate assumptions and rebuilt term premia. U.S. investment grade credit is forecast at 6.6%, partly lifted by the wave of bond issuance from technology hyperscalers financing AI data centre buildouts. U.S. high yield credit rises to 7.2% from 6.5%, with a fair value spread of 440 basis points and improved underlying index quality cited as key drivers. In the alternatives space, the report delivers its most significant upgrade to diversified hedge funds, raising the return assumption by 230 basis points to 7.1%, reflecting sustained alpha generation trends and the higher rate environment. Private equity is projected to return 10.2%, though the report is explicit that this return potential is now tied to repeatable operational value creation rather than financial leverage. Global core infrastructure is upgraded to 7.5% from 6.0%, a direct beneficiary of manufacturing reshoring and supply chain rerouting. U.S. core real estate is expected to return 8.5%, while broad basket commodities are projected at 5.2%, with gold upgraded 90 basis points to 5.9%. In a notable institutional first, J.P. Morgan has introduced a long-term return estimate for Bitcoin at approximately 10% annualised. The firm was careful to note that Bitcoin has not yet been incorporated into its main portfolio covariance matrix, reflecting the asset’s still-evolving role in institutional allocation frameworks. A central theme of the 2027 LTCMAs is the inadequacy of a simple 60/40 stock-bond portfolio in the current environment. Higher inflation volatility has increased the correlation between equities and bonds, eroding the diversification benefit that made the traditional balanced portfolio so effective in the low-inflation decade prior to 2022. J.P. Morgan’s response is the 60/40+ framework, which incorporates a 30% allocation to diversified alternatives alongside the traditional equity and bond sleeves. Under this construction, the projected annual return rises from 7.1% to 7.7%, and the Sharpe ratio improves by approximately 20% compared to the simple 60/40 approach. The alternatives allocation draws on hedge funds for alpha generation, real assets for inflation resilience, and infrastructure for income stability tied to real economic activity. J.P. Morgan’s 2027 Long-Term Capital Market Assumptions deliver a broadly optimistic long-term investment thesis anchored in AI-driven productivity, a generational reset in bond yields, and upgraded corporate profitability, but the firm is equally clear that the path forward will be bumpier than the headline return numbers suggest. Elevated stock-bond correlations, persistent inflation volatility, and the operational demands of private market investing mean that achieving these projected returns will require disciplined diversification, active risk management, and a willingness to move beyond the comfort of traditional portfolio construction. Explore how Sadia Halal, an MBRF company, is moving beyond exports, expanding local operations and building out a regional platform to grow in the Middle East. International growth is challenging—especially when you’re adding operations more than 7,000 miles from your headquarters. That was the case for Sadia Halal and its parent company, MBRF, as it restructured its operations in 2026 to focus on its more locally anchored footprint in the Middle East to address the demand for halal protein, while entering into a dedicated supply agreement with its parent company for the supply of poultry and beef. The company’s ambition goes beyond supplying the Middle East, bringing halal products to markets around the world. Learn more about how J.P. Morgan is helping MBRF and Sadia Halal scale globally by combining deep local coverage with global capabilities—supporting their growth beyond any single transaction. Sadia Halal is one of the largest halal food platforms worldwide, offering frozen poultry, ready-to-prepare products, vegetables, fries and other proteins produced in accordance with Islamic dietary laws. Part of MBRF, a global multiprotein company, Sadia Halal was established in April 2026 through a partnership with the Public Investment Fund (PIF), the sovereign wealth fund of Saudi Arabia, to accelerate growth in the global halal market and strengthen its regional footprint. “Sadia Halal leverages local market knowledge and international standards to deliver solutions that meet the needs of retailers, restaurant chains and households across Middle East Countries,” said Fabio Mariano, MBRF Vice President for the halal market and CEO of Sadia Halal. “Today, we are proud to be the market leader in the chicken category, as well as the preferred brand of consumers in the region.” 

Sadia Halal operates as part of MBRF, one of the largest global food companies, formed in 2025 via the merger of Brazilian corporations Marfrig and BRF. Building on over five decades of Sadia brand presence and consumer experience in the Middle East, the platform combines regional production and distribution with the industrial capabilities of its parent company. The number of Muslims around the world grew from 1.7 billion to 2.0 billion between 2010 and 2020—a 21% increase—according to Pew Research Center. That population growth, combined with rising consumer expectations for quality, transparency and convenience, is fueling demand for halal food products. “Now is the time to invest in the halal markets,” Mariano said. “Halal products represent close to $2 trillion in spending, and the halal food segment is expected to reach $1.5 trillion in the coming years.” “Brazilian companies that have scaled internationally tend to combine strong competitive advantages in their home market with the ability to localize their business model,” said Thiago Carvalho, Deputy Head of Investment Banking, Brazil, at J.P. Morgan. “Sadia Halal is a great example of that.” “We have the Brazilian knowledge of how to produce chicken,” said Marquinhos Molina, Chairman of Sadia Halal and CEO of MBRF Saudi Arabia. “We also have a deep knowledge on the local markets where we act—how people cook, share meals and celebrate.” The company’s vertical business model is also integral to its success. In 2014, Sadia Halal began shifting from an export-driven model to a more local operation to expand regional production capacity, broaden its footprint and stay closer to its customer base. Sadia Halal’s platform is designed to serve multiple channels, including retailers and restaurant chains. The company operates facilities in Saudi Arabia and the UAE and distributes across its network in the region. Sadia Halal also leverages MBRF’s operations in Brazil, where multiple facilities are approved to export to the Middle East. “The combination of our global know-how paired with local knowledge makes Sadia one of the most powerful brands in local food,” Molina said. “The more we expand our operations internationally, our strategic and financial needs get more sophisticated and complex. It’s better to have a bank with a global reach and very strong execution expertise.” “What differentiates J.P. Morgan is our ability to serve our clients in Brazil globally across all types of products, from their day-to-day needs to the most important and relevant transactions,” Carvalho said. The firm has worked closely with MBRF and Sadia Halal since the platform’s formation, providing strategic guidance and execution expertise to MBRF across strategic transactions, including mergers and acquisitions, equity capital markets and debt capital markets. “The more we expand our operations internationally, our strategic and financial needs get more sophisticated and complex,” Mariano said. “It’s better to have a bank with a global reach and very strong execution expertise—not to mention a long-lasting relationship with MBRF and a track record of successful transactions over the years.” “We have a long-term relationship with J.P. Morgan and believe there’s nobody better to expand our business globally,” Molina said. J.P. Morgan supports clients as they expand across borders—combining local market capabilities with global execution expertise. title: A silver soup tureen once owned by JP Morgan could fetch $8 million at a Christie’s auction - Aurora Sentinel
content: LONDON | It’s a perfect gift for the host with the most. Sign up for our free newsletter to receive the latest news Sign up for our free newsletter to receive the latest news A huge silver soup tureen once owned by financier J.P. Morgan up for sale, with an estimated price of up to 6 million pounds (almost $8 million). More than a foot and a half long (46 centimeters) long and weighing in at 44 pounds (20 kilograms), the Meissonnier Tureen is the star of a Dec. 1 auction at Christie’s in London. Made in the 1730s by the French artist and goldsmith Juste-Aurèle Meissonnier in a flamboyant rococo style, it was “designed to astonish,” according to Christie’s specialist Isabelle Cartier-Stone. Shaped like a stylized shell, it has a cover encrusted with detailed silver plants and animals, including “a duck, a crab, a fish, an oyster, and a snail among an artichoke and other leafy vegetables,” according to the catalog. The tureen’s owners have included British aristocrats, Russian statesmen and the American banker John Pierpont Morgan. It is one of a pair split up after they were auctioned together in 1977, with the other in the Cleveland Museum of Art in Ohio. It is being sold as part of a trove of silver owned by the Blaquier-Arrieta family of wealthy Argentine collectors and has a presale estimate of between 4 million pounds and 6 million pounds ($5.25 million and $7.86 million). title: HSBC, JP Morgan settle first live digital gold collateral trades - Ledger Insights
content: The World Gold Council announced the first live transactions for Pooled Gold Interests (PGI) between HSBC, JP Morgan and StoneX, a little over a year after it first proposed the concept in a September 2025 white paper. The Wholesale Digital Gold pilot involved trading, settlement and the use of gold as collateral, which is a key driver behind the initiative. ICE Benchmark Administration (IBA) is the platform operator and Baton Systems is the technology provider. Gold is a significant market worth around $28 trillion in total, with around half of that considered investable. About $8 trillion is in the form of physical bars, coins, gold ETFs and over the counter private investments, with central banks managing $5 trillion and derivatives worth more than a trillion. The challenge with physical gold is it sits at custodians, and moving it is not that easy. Yet owners want to use it as collateral, and the UK’s Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) is exploring how to make that happen. Pooled Gold Interests aim to combine quick transfers with a proprietary interest in the gold, which might make central counterparties (CCPs) more willing to accept it as collateral. It’s not that gold isn’t currently electronically traded. The challenge is the formats. To transfer gold quickly, most is held “unallocated” with a bank, meaning it is a claim on the bank as opposed to outright ownership of the bars. In London those claims are mainly on Citi, HSBC, ICBC Standard Bank, JP Morgan and UBS. Because of the bank counterparty risk, this form of gold is not eligible as CCP collateral in the UK and EU. By contrast there is far less risk if identified gold bars are held at a custodian, but there’s friction in transferring it. This is referred to as “allocated” gold and CME Clearing is one of the few to accept this as collateral. The World Gold Council’s PGI pilot introduces a third path that addresses the counterparty risk while making gold easier to move and settle. The FCA is expressly exploring gold tokenization. Yet the PGI pilot does not use tokens, even though it uses a distributed ledger. Baton Systems told Ledger Insights the PGIs were created on its permissioned DLT, which also handled the transfers, settlement and the collateral pledge. Baton is known for its Core Collateral and Core FX solutions, with HSBC as an anchor client for Core FX, which is now the foundation of OSTTRA’s PvP offering. Core FX likewise uses DLT for workflow purposes rather than tokens, and several years ago HSBC’s Mark Williamson outlined some of the benefits of sidestepping tokenization to Ledger Insights, noting that tokenization can add an extra settlement step and create fragmented liquidity. Since then HSBC has launched its own gold tokenization offering, both for wholesale clients and for retail in Hong Kong. Want the full story? When everything shifts, the edge is seeing what others miss. J.P. Morgan NextList 2027 offers a collection of books and experiences that shine a light on what’s next. Thirteen titles exploring the ideas, people and perspectives shaping the year ahead. Danny Meyer, restaurateur, hospitality pioneer and founder of Shake Shack, shares hard-won lessons on how to maintain a culture of excellence at scale. Filled with candid stories from his time building a celebrated restaurant group and creating a global ecosystem, he offers a practical playbook for building resilient teams, raising standards and sustaining what he calls “Enlightened Hospitality.” The result is an energizing read for leaders determined to build enduring businesses where relationships and values scale alongside performance. Investment experts Jenny Harrington and Rebecca Patterson gather the candid advice 25 seasoned finance professionals share with their own family and close friends. Through personal stories, the contributors explain their practical approaches to complex markets, including how to stay disciplined through volatility, avoid common traps and build habits that compound over time. As Wall Street grows increasingly complex and the largest wealth transfer in history unfolds, this book captures the investment wisdom typically reserved for the family dinner table or a coffee with a dear friend. Authored by the founder of Dimensional Fund Advisors and a pioneer of index investing, Stay Calm is a guide to building wealth rooted in the science of markets, not speculation. Drawing on decades at the center of modern finance, David Booth explains why markets absorb information quickly, and why that can be an advantage for disciplined investors. Focusing on diversification, patience and how to avoid common emotional mistakes, Stay Calm argues that while uncertainty is a permanent feature of markets and life, it can be a source of opportunity for those who can keep their cool. The design editor of New York magazine and Curbed and former style director at Harper’s Bazaar unveils 80 defining moments in department store Bergdorf Goodman’s 125-year history. From designer debuts to its legendary windows, she describes how the Fifth Avenue institution helped shape the language of modern luxury. With pictures from Bergdorf’s longtime window photographer Ricky Zehavi and reflections from voices such as Rihanna, Thom Browne and Michael Kors, Very Bergdorf is a love letter to this retail landmark. The owner of the Baltimore Orioles and the co-founder and co-chairman of The Carlyle Group shares true stories from the business of sports ownership through conversations with some of America’s most influential franchise owners. Behind the very public valuations and blockbuster dealmaking is what fans don’t always see: owners thinking about how to build culture and community around a team and its city. Rubenstein gives readers an inside look at the modern sports ecosystem – including the financial playbook, the dynamics of media rights and betting, the fan economy and more – that will appeal to anyone interested in sports as an asset class and platform for connection. A senior researcher at Oxford University’s Institute for Ethics in AI tackles one of today’s most urgent questions: How do we prepare the next generation for a world reshaped by artificial intelligence? Taking a clear-eyed yet optimistic approach, he explains how new tools are changing the nature of work and what that means for education, skill-building and resilience. Written for parents, students and leaders navigating the disruption, the book offers an evidence-based framework that considers job opportunities beyond their titles and helps the workforce of the future adapt to new capabilities. In Situated, the psychologist and bestselling author of Grit shifts the focus from perseverance to environment for achieving your goals. With in-depth research, Duckworth proves how the people around you and where you spend your time can change your behavior – and how high performers design environments that make excellence easier. With practical insights on reducing temptation, solving problems and building the right circles of peers and mentors, she offers guidance on improving outcomes by changing your situation, not just your mindset. Investor and enterprise builder Alec Litowitz argues that in a world defined by volatility, a high adaptability quotient (AQ) can give anyone an edge. In his new book, he guides readers on decision making in times of uncertainty, with a focus on how to think clearly, act decisively and pivot when necessary. As artificial intelligence and rapid media cycles reshape how we process information, he makes the case that AQ is both a learnable discipline and a key advantage for future leaders. By Mory Sacko, Bénédicte Bortoli and Émilie Rouquette In his debut cookbook, the Michelin-starred chef and founder of acclaimed Paris restaurant Mosuke shares recipes and stories that draw on his African heritage, passion for Japan and French education. Winner of the Michelin Young Chef Award for France in 2021 at the age of 28, Mory Sacko pairs more than 60 seasonal recipes with essays that explain the methods and ideas that shape his distinctive style. Beautifully photographed, the book also captures his philosophy of hospitality that includes welcoming restaurant guests as if they were in his home. Leadership scholar Linda A. Hill, Harvard Business School researcher Emily Tedards and former Microsoft innovation executive Jason Wild show how innovation only happens when leaders build effective systems for collaboration and learning. Highlighting the three roles leaders must play: architect, bridger and catalyst – they profile innovators across industries and geographies who display the skills and attitude needed to inspire future innovation. Genius at Scale is a practical guide for founders and executives who want to turn experimentation into durable impact. Authored by Singaporean design writer Daven Wu, a longtime collaborator with architect and designer André Fu, this volume offers an intimate look at one of hospitality design’s most influential contemporary voices. Fu approaches hotels as immersive destinations shaped by mood, memory and place. Conversations with creative figures who have influenced Fu deepen the cultural context, while rich photography and previously unpublished material reveal the designer’s process. For readers who travel for aesthetics as much as geography, André Fu: A Designer’s Vision proves why thoughtful design alone can be a good reason to embark on a new journey. By Clare Foster (introduction) and Juliet Roberts and Colleen Morris, et al. (texts) The garden editor of House & Garden tours more than 40 private gardens rarely seen by the public, spaces shaped as intensely by vision and craft as any interior or collection. The book highlights today’s leading designers and owner-makers through large-format photography and narratives that explain each garden’s story, structure and signature plantings. From intimate, locally rooted landscapes to more architectural, Mediterranean terraces, the book shows beautiful convergences of horticulture, design, luxury and creativity. The NBA All-Star and New York Knicks captain writes a heartfelt picture book about trying new things, learning through setbacks and discovering strengths over time. Told through Brunson’s childhood experiments across various sports, the story emphasizes discipline, teamwork and confidence, highlighting the importance of small choices: to show up, practice and stay resilient when it would be easier to quit. The book is an encouraging reminder to kids that the journey to finding “your thing” is often where the most important lessons are learned. Six destinations worth your attention, from a new longevity destination in Phuket to a Venetian palazzo devoted to craft. In 2026, Venice’s Palazzo Pisani Moretta entered a new chapter as a cultural foundation created by Belgian fashion designer Dries Van Noten and his partner, Patrick Vangheluwe. It centers on craftsmanship in the broadest sense – work made by hand, guided by skill and soul – bringing together exhibitions, residencies and talks that blur the lines between fashion, design, art, jewelry, photography, glass and ceramics. Its opening presentation, The Only True Protest Is Beauty, sets the tone: a cross-disciplinary exploration of beauty and creative heritage. Swiss longevity pioneer Clinique La Prairie has created an immersive retreat set within the lush surroundings of Tri Vananda in Phuket. Guided by its signature CLP Longevity Method, the program brings together advanced medical science with personalized nutrition, movement and well-being, with a focus on prevention, resilience and long-term vitality. The experience helps guests understand their biology, strengthen their daily habits and return home with a clear plan for lasting health. Following Anji in China and Phuket, another Clinique La Prairie health resort is set to open at AMAALA, on Saudi Arabia’s Red Sea coast, in 2027. Designed as a major hub for astronomy education and dark-sky preservation, the International Dark Sky Discovery Center, opening in early 2027, will make the night sky an immersive, hands-on experience. Planned highlights include a Dark Sky Observatory with the largest telescope in the Greater Phoenix area, a planetarium with tilted-dome technology, an LED-screen theater, interactive exhibit halls and family-friendly exploration stations. With science-based programming and partnerships across education, the center will also support astrotourism through lectures, public viewing nights and community events that reconnect visitors with the wonder of truly dark skies. Set on Norway’s dramatic northern coast, The Whale is an experience and knowledge center designed to deepen understanding of whale biology, behavior, evolution and ecology while inspiring ocean conservation. The forthcoming space, set to open in June 2027, is conceived as a multi-sensory journey that merges science with art, inviting visitors to feel the scale, intelligence and mystery of the world’s largest mammals and to reflect on humanity’s relationship with the sea. With architecture as striking as its setting, The Whale will be a destination where education, empathy and awe meet. Suzhou Museum of Contemporary Art is a new cultural landmark on the right bank of Jinji Lake that was designed by renowned Danish architecture firm Bjarke Ingels Group and spans 59,500 square meters, with approximately 11,300 square meters of exhibition space. Located in Suzhou Industrial Park beside the “Suzhou’s Eye” Ferris wheel, this large-scale public museum allows visitors to wander through a garden of pavilions and courtyards connected by art-filled galleries and porticoes. A decade in the making, La Hacienda by tequila brand Clase Azul México is a new large-scale cultural estate and production complex in Los Altos de Jalisco. Developed in collaboration with five of Mexico’s acclaimed architecture firms, the 50-acre estate brings together working distillation and bottling facilities with artisan workshops dedicated to the handmade ceramic decanters that define the brand. Visitors can explore curated spaces that highlight regional heritage while hospitality elements, including a restaurant, OYA, focused on traditional Mexican cuisine, complete the experience. Four productions taking the Broadway stage this season, from three new musicals to Shakespeare reimagined. Tony Award winner Jamie Lloyd's production of William Shakespeare's Much Ado About Nothing stars Tom Hiddleston (Tony Award nominee, Olivier Award winner and Golden Globe Award winner) as Benedick, and Hayley Atwell (three-time Olivier Award nominee, Standard Theatre Award winner and Golden Globe Award nominee) in her Broadway debut as Beatrice. This giddily funny and beautifully rendered battle of wits comes to Broadway for a limited 10-week engagement, ending Sunday, January 10, 2027. A new stage musical celebrates the life and music of Dolly Parton, following her journey from the Smoky Mountains to global superstardom. Built around hits like “Jolene,” “9 to 5,” “I Will Always Love You” and new songs Parton wrote for the musical, the show blends joy with depth, exploring the grit, generosity and ambition behind Parton’s inspiring career. With direction by Bartlett Sher and a book by Dolly Parton and Maria S. Schlatter, DOLLY is a crowd-pleaser and a portrait of continual reinvention. A record-breaking London sensation and winner of seven Olivier Awards, Paddington The Musical brings a beloved character to life through extraordinary theatrical innovation. Now headed to Broadway in spring 2027, this production is imaginative and optimistic, with a timeless message about kindness, belonging and adventure. Experience Prince’s legacy in Purple Rain, the electrifying new musical inspired by his Grammy-winning album and Oscar-winning film, featuring more than 20 iconic hits, including “When Doves Cry” and “The Beautiful Ones.” Set in Minneapolis in 1984, during the rise of a new era of music television, the show stars Jordan Fisher as the magnetic rock musician. A visionary team brings Prince’s world to the stage, led by Tony-nominated director Saheem Ali, librettist Peter Duchan, choreographer Ebony Williams, music director Jason Michael Webb, and Prince music advisors and longtime collaborators Bobby Z and Morris Hayes. Two California wineries in Napa Valley and Sonoma County, each blending innovation, artistry and legacy. Winemaker Jesse Katz, named to Forbes’ 30 Under 30 and Wine Enthusiast’s Winemaker of the Year, has created more than 60 perfect 100-point wines. He founded Aperture on the belief that wine is an artistic expression. He draws inspiration from his father, celebrated photographer Andy Katz, and their foundation was shaped by years of travel and hands-on wine education, tasting with iconic producers in legendary cellars across Europe. The result is a winery that feels less like a traditional tasting room and more like a creative platform – where art, nature and craftsmanship meet, and the wines are the entry point into a broader world. The TOR story began long before the first vintage was bottled. For half a century, Tor Kenward has been part of the fabric of Napa Valley. What started as a lifelong passion evolved into TOR Wines in 2001. Today, with more than 30 100-point scores and international acclaim, TOR focuses on single-vineyard Cabernet Sauvignon and Chardonnay from Napa’s most storied sites made in very limited quantities. Family-owned and sourcing exclusively from vineyards widely regarded as Napa Valley’s First Growths, TOR continues to write the next chapter in Napa’s modern legacy. Not working with us yet? Update: The report has been corrected to mention that Fidelity Investments is bringing tokenized crypto ETPs, not tokenized shares, to OKXICE TSV. Fidelity Investments has decided to step into the tokenization zone from which JPMorgan Chase (NYSE: JPM) has retreated. JPMorgan is a publicly listed company and its shares are traded under the ticker symbol JPM on the New York Stock Exchange (NYSE). But when a crypto platform proposed to list a tokenized version of the JPM stock, the Wall Street giant opposed the plan. However, Fidelity Investments has decided to join this tokenized securities program as an issuer. This shows the asset manager isn't hesitant to tap an innovative financial technology that the world's largest bank is unwilling to engage with. Tokenization is the process of using blockchain technology to turn real‑world assets (RWAs) such as stocks, real estate, government bonds, etc. into digital tokens, which can be traded fractionally, 24/7. While the stock tokens offer traders from outside the U.S. indirect exposure to the American stock market, they don't offer shareholder rights such as ownership, voting, etc., like original stocks do. The Securities and Exchange Commission's (SEC) innovation exemption published in September lets crypto exchanges offer tokenized U.S. stocks without registering as exchanges. But the exemption also allows companies to object to their shares being tokenized by third parties. One such proposed tokenized stock trading platform is OKXICE TSV, a 50-50 joint venture between the NYSE parent Intercontinental Exchange (NYSE: ICE) and the crypto exchange OKX. But several companies such as JPMorgan have opposed the plan, protesting the listing of the tokenized version of their stocks. In fact, 67 issuers had filed objections according to the OKXICE public notice on Nov. 20. Among the leading protestors are: Bitcoin rallies as Nvidia brings back Jensen Huang Halted food company's Bitcoin losses swell to $51M As OKXICE got launched on Nov. 23, the crypto platform confirmed 113 assets that eligible U.S. customers can trade 24/7. Fidelity Investments joins as an issuer of tokenized crypto ETPs on OKXICE. The asset manager is a privately held company and it is involved in the tokenization of crypto ETPs that will trade on OKXICE TSV. title: JP Morgan Supplies $90M Refi for Murray Hill Multifamily Tower - Commercial Observer
content: Brause Realty has secured a $90 million loan to refinance a newly built luxury apartment tower in Midtown East, Commercial Observer has learned. J.P. Morgan Chase provided the loan for the developer’s 157-unit the Lotus property in Manhattan’s Murray Hill neighborhood, a project completed in early 2026. Brause Realty also landed a $75 million construction loan from J.P. Morgan for the project in 2024, CO first reported at the time. Cushman & Wakefield negotiated the refi with a team consisting of Gideon Gil, Zach Kraft, Cecelia Galligan and Crawford Bundy. “The property’s strong leasing performance, exceptional amenities and long-term tax benefits helped secure attractive financing terms, reflecting continued lender demand for well-positioned multifamily properties in New York City,” Gil, executive vice chairman with C&W, said in a statement. Located at 255 East 39th Street, the 20-story property has 109 market-rate apartments and 48 units designated as affordable housing, along with 3,900 square feet of ground-floor retail space. Resident amenities include a rooftop lounge, coworking spaces, a fitness center, a yoga studio, a sports simulator and a screening room. The Brause family acquired properties along Second Avenue and East 39th Street in 1942 before expanding ownership in the ensuing decades and completed assemblage for the project in 2021. “The Lotus represents an important milestone for our family and reflects our long-standing commitment to investing in New York City,” David Brause, president of Brause Realty, said in a statement. “We’re proud to have delivered a premier residential property that brings high-quality housing and exceptional amenities to the Murray Hill neighborhood.” J.P. Morgan did not immediately return a request for comment. Andrew Coen can be reached at acoen@commercialobserver.com. Read the latest edition of the Commercial Observer online!

The impact of rising rates is likely to be uneven, with capital-intensive sectors and highly leveraged companies facing greater pressure. With the Federal Reserve (Fed) expected to hike rates in December amid persistent inflation and AI-driven growth, companies are positioning for higher borrowing costs. However, the impact of the interest rate outlook will not be uniform across sectors, with outcomes likely dependent on balance-sheet leverage, capital intensity and proximity to the AI boom. “The first-order impact of higher rates on corporate interest expenses should be gradual because debt is permanently fixed and long-dated,” explained Kamal Tamboli, who covers Equity Strategy and Global Thematic Research at J.P. Morgan. “Although higher rates could have negative second-order effects on the consumer and AI capital spending, healthy corporate balance sheets, elevated margins and ample household liquidity should limit the sensitivity, with greater pressure concentrated among smaller companies, highly leveraged businesses and capital-intensive industries outside the AI buildout.” What sectors are best positioned to succeed in a higher rate environment? “We see greater pressure concentrated among smaller companies, highly leveraged businesses and capital-intensive industries outside the AI buildout.” Equity Strategy and Global Thematic Research, J.P. Morgan Some automotive companies are expected to weather rising rates better than others. “Even as inflation and affordability pressures keep auto industry sales subdued, we see the automotive ecosystem bifurcating along two fault lines: balance-sheet dependence and exposure to the AI growth engine pushing rates higher,” said Rajat Gupta, head of the U.S. Autos equity research team at J.P. Morgan. For instance, auto suppliers that are expanding beyond vehicle propulsion into modular turbine generators and gensets — equipment that supports the AI buildout — could benefit in the current macro environment if the AI boom continues. Conversely, rental companies with substantial fleet financing and corporate debt may have to grapple with higher interest costs. Franchised dealers, too, could face higher financing and debt costs, but steady revenue from parts and repair services could help cushion the impact. “Net-net, the driver of higher rates matters as much as the level. Companies tethered to the narrow AI growth engine can outrun higher rates, while those dependent on a squeezed consumer and leverage are positioned unfavorably,” Gupta said. “Even as inflation and affordability pressures keep auto industry sales subdued, we see the automotive ecosystem bifurcating along two fault lines: balance-sheet dependence and exposure to the AI growth engine pushing rates higher.” Head of the U.S. Autos equity research team, J.P. Morgan For food producers and retailers, the burden of rising rates will likely take the form of higher borrowing costs. “For many U.S. food companies, balance sheets carry higher-than-targeted levels of debt, and elevated dividend payout ratios constrain companies’ ability to reduce debt. As a result, a rising rate environment presents an earnings headwind for food companies as debt is rolled over,” said Thomas Palmer, head of the U.S. Food Producers and Food Retailers team at J.P. Morgan. On the other hand, agricultural companies, particularly larger producers, could see a modest benefit from higher rates. “This is because distribution margins tend to be larger when interest rates rise to reflect the higher cost of carrying inventory,” Palmer explained. For retailers and leisure providers, higher rates are more likely to affect costs associated with the goods or services they sell, rather than curb consumer spending. This is especially as consumers have remained remarkably resilient in the face of inflation, supported in part by wealth gains and savings drawdowns. According to Fed data, U.S. households have created approximately $80 trillion in net wealth since 2019, with that figure rising 7% year over year in 2026 alone. “As such, the greatest risk is concentrated in companies with outsized leverage ratios, as well as retailers of big-ticket items, whose end-market purchasing power is reliant on lower interest rates,” said Matthew Boss, head of Department Stores, Specialty Softlines and Leisure at J.P. Morgan. Electricity prices have risen alongside interest rates, potentially helping renewable energy projects offset higher financing costs through increased power revenues. “That said, based on evidence from when interest rates increased several years ago, we expect a headwind for the residential solar sector, which could exhibit waning consumer sentiment,” said Mark Strouse, a senior analyst on the U.S. Clean Energy, Power Infrastructure and Sustainable Investing team at J.P. Morgan. Within utility-scale renewables, smaller developers may be more exposed to higher rates if they have not arranged long-term financing or secured favorable Power Purchase Agreement (PPA) prices — the pre-negotiated rate at which electricity is sold — for projects under construction. “This could lead to further consolidation of the space by larger developers with stronger contracting wherewithal and access to capital,” Strouse observed. By contrast, upstream (exploration and production) and downstream (refining and marketing) oil and gas companies are expected to be relatively insulated from rising rates. “Energy equities have historically been one of the least rate-sensitive sectors in the broader market as the stocks are much more correlated to commodity price expectations and short-duration cash flows,” noted Arun Jayaram, head of the U.S. Exploration, Production, Oilfield Services and Equipment Research teams at J.P. Morgan. “However, the rising cost of capital, as well as access to capital, could be headwinds to companies levered to the AI buildout, such as those providing behind-the-meter solutions that power data centers.” J.P. Morgan Global Research expects rising rates to support large-cap banks in the near term. This is largely through higher net interest income (NII) — the difference between the revenue a bank generates from interest-bearing assets and the interest it pays on deposits and borrowings — although the benefit could be tempered by elevated deposit competition. “Additionally, while higher rates modestly weigh on capital, the impact is manageable. Plus, there are other factors that could also affect bank stocks, including the impact of rising rates on the stock market and hence on capital markets activity,” said Vivek Juneja, a senior analyst covering large U.S. Banks at J.P. Morgan. “The key longer-term concern is that a sustained series of hikes could slow the economy. This could drive concerns about markets-related revenues, notably in investment banking, and hence make the sector choppy.” Mid- and small-cap banks may also see near-term earnings support. “However, higher incremental funding costs could potentially weigh on NII despite asset repricing benefits,” said Anthony Elian, who covers U.S. Mid- and Small-Cap Banks at J.P. Morgan. Additionally, elevated long-term yields pressure securities valuations, while increased borrowing costs could dampen loan demand, particularly across commercial real estate and mortgage-related businesses. “Overall, while additional rate hikes should benefit asset-sensitive banks in the near term, we believe deposit pricing discipline, securities exposure and the ability to sustain loan growth without deterioration in credit quality will increasingly differentiate performance,” Elian said. For non-bank lenders, the impact will depend largely on their balance sheets. “Floating-rate lenders with clean credit books should see higher NII. On the other hand, rate-sensitive, volume-driven businesses and commercial mortgage REITs with large non-accrual books face the biggest headwinds,” said Richard Shane, head of the Consumer & Specialty Finance team at J.P. Morgan. “This is because higher rates suppress origination and transaction volumes, and push out the loan resolutions their recovery depends on.” Sustained higher rates could weigh on biotech companies, particularly those still in the development stage, which typically depend on external funding. “While we do not believe the sector’s access to the capital markets will close, the pace of financing could slow and the bar for financing could be higher,” said Jessica Fye, a senior analyst covering Large-Cap Biotechnology at J.P. Morgan. “That said, we continue to see a fundraising pathway for companies that deliver compelling clinical data and strong launches,” added Anupam Rama, who covers U.S. SMID Biotechnology at J.P. Morgan. Tighter biotech funding could in turn dampen demand for life science tools and diagnostics. “This matters because biotech is a key demand pillar across preclinical services, outsourced R&D, lab instruments and consumables, and specialty workflows,” said Casey Woodring, who covers U.S. Life Science Tools & Diagnostics at J.P. Morgan. In particular, higher financing costs could slow discretionary outsourcing, leaving contract research organizations (CROs) — third-party firms that provide research and clinical trial services — negatively exposed. Pharmaceutical companies, by contrast, are expected to be relatively immune to higher rates. “Leverage across the sector remains very manageable, and we do not expect any significant impact on M&A activity. If anything, lower valuations could accelerate deal volume,” said Chris Schott, a senior analyst covering the U.S. Diversified Biopharma Sector at J.P. Morgan. “Overall, with fundamentals in a good place and the sector not sensitive to macro challenges, we see pharma names performing well in a rising rate environment.” “While we do not believe the biotech’s sector’s access to the capital markets will close, the pace of financing could slow and the bar for financing could be higher.” Senior analyst covering Large-Cap Biotechnology, J.P. Morgan As semiconductors and related capital equipment are capital-intensive, they have historically been sensitive to rate fluctuations. “We believe higher rates generally represent a headwind across the sector, with some verticals being more impacted than others. This is as higher rates raise borrowing costs, pressure end-market demand, encourage more cautious inventory management and raise the overall bar for customers to continue spending aggressively on AI infrastructure,” said Harlan Sur, head of the U.S. Semiconductor and Semiconductor Capital Equipment team at J.P. Morgan. J.P. Morgan Global Research sees analog semiconductors being particularly exposed because of their ties to cyclical end-markets such as industrials and autos. Here, higher rates could weigh on customer spending and prolong inventory drawdowns. AI and compute companies could also face greater scrutiny. “Elevated rates could force hyperscalers and frontier AI customers to slow, phase or reprioritize spending if expected returns do not justify the scale of upfront investment, especially given the rising dependence on external financing,” Sur added. By comparison, Electronic Design Automation (EDA) tools and process control equipment may prove more resilient as spending in these areas is closely tied to R&D budgets. “These budgets tend to be durable through macroeconomic cycles, given their importance in driving continued advancements in chip design, technology roadmaps and manufacturing yields,” Sur explained. Beyond sector-specific dynamics, the shape of the yield curve — which measures how interest rates rise across different maturities — could also determine which companies are best positioned. “The principal risks are that earnings growth weakens, the bond selloff becomes abrupt and volatile, or geopolitical escalation in the Middle East creates a more severe inflation and growth shock,” Tamboli said. The Federal Reserve voted to pause in October amidst hot inflation prints and a resilient job market. When is the next hike expected to take place? Global bond yields have repriced higher on hawkish “higher-for-longer” policy expectations, elevated energy prices and geopolitical uncertainty, reshaping markets into year-end. title: ‘Grossly missed expectations’ Down Under: Consing’s former employer J.P. Morgan flags ACEN’s ₱2.35B Australian loss, questions provisions - Bilyonaryo Business
content: Ayala Group’s Australian solar farms are generating more electricity, but ACEN chairman Cezar Consing and president and CEO Eric Francia have yet to stop the continuous bleeding Down Under. The Ayala-controlled renewable energy company lost ₱2.35 billion from its Australian operations in the first nine months of 2026, more than three times the ₱710 million loss recorded for the whole of 2025. The worsening performance has drawn criticism from J.P. Morgan, where Consing spent nearly two decades and once headed its Asia-Pacific investment banking business. “Australia still remains the key sore point,” J.P. Morgan said in its November 11 report, describing ACEN’s nine-month earnings as having “grossly missed expectations.” The investment bank blamed weak electricity prices, stalled power supply contracts and defective cables at New England Solar for much of the disappointment. ACEN’s core profit fell 46 percent to ₱2.4 billion in the first nine months, with the company posting a ₱154 million core loss in the third quarter. Even a strong recovery in its Philippine operations was not enough to offset the Australian weakness. “We anticipate downward earnings revisions following the miss,” J.P. Morgan said. The bank also warned of a negative market reaction but maintained its Neutral rating and ₱2.90 share price target. ACEN’s Australian operations recorded a combined ₱3.18 billion in losses attributable to shareholders in 2024, 2025 and the first nine months of 2026. ACEN’s Australian solar farms generated 48 percent more power in the first nine months of 2026, reaching 1,303 gigawatt-hours as output increased at New England Solar and Stubbo Solar in New South Wales. Revenue attributable to ACEN jumped 73 percent to ₱3.1 billion, while attributable earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization (EBITDA) rose 49 percent to ₱1.7 billion. But higher electricity output and revenue have yet to translate into bottom-line profits. J.P. Morgan noted that Australia’s EBITDA for the first nine months reached just 57 percent of its full-year forecast. The bank attributed weak electricity prices partly to coal-fired power plants staying open longer than expected and the rapid expansion of battery storage. Both developments have also made it harder for ACEN to secure attractive long-term electricity contracts. ACEN’s problems extend beyond weak electricity prices. At New England Solar, defective electrical cables have forced the company to recognize additional charges and undertake repairs, which management expects to complete by December 2026. Another setback came in July when Australian electricity retailer ZEN Energy entered voluntary administration. ACEN terminated its long-term electricity supply agreement with ZEN, which had about eight and a half years remaining, and replaced it with a one-year transitional arrangement while seeking a longer-term deal. The setbacks have prompted J.P. Morgan to question whether ACEN has fully accounted for the financial impact of troubled projects across its renewable energy portfolio. “Impairments YTD across the Philippines, Vietnam and Australia raise questions on whether provisions are sufficient,” the bank said. In simpler terms, J.P. Morgan is questioning whether ACEN has recognized enough of the decline in value of its troubled assets, or whether further accounting charges may be necessary. ACEN reported a consolidated net loss of ₱609 million in the third quarter, reflecting charges associated with the Australian cable defects and a damaged wind turbine in the Philippines. With Australian losses mounting, J.P. Morgan has a pointed message for ACEN’s management: secure better electricity contracts and demonstrate “more disciplined capital spending” before expecting a more favorable assessment. The warning comes from Consing’s former employer, where he worked from 1985 to 2004. He joined ACEN’s board in 2021, became vice chairman in 2022 and took over as chairman in April 2024. Francia has overseen ACEN’s renewable energy expansion, including its entry into Australia in 2018 through a partnership with UPC Renewables. ACEN completed its takeover of the Australian business in February 2023. The company has since established a substantial presence in Australia, with its New England and Stubbo solar projects boasting a combined capacity of more than 1,000 megawatts. For Consing and Francia, the challenge is no longer building solar farms or generating more electricity. It is making those investments pay off.—Bilyonaryo.com Atras ka, boy! President Donald Trump's renewed support for limiting U.S. credit-card interest rates to 10% has brought earnings risks into focus for Citigroup C, JPMorgan Chase JPM and Capital One Financial COF. Citigroup runs a large U.S. Consumer Cards business spanning general-purpose and private-label cards, while JPMorgan operates a major card franchise within its Consumer & Community Banking division. Capital One has significant exposure to credit-card lending, particularly following its acquisition of Discover Financial Services. All three companies benefit from interest earned on revolving card balances, leaving them exposed to potential revenue and margin pressures from any mandatory reduction in borrowing rates. On Nov. 21, Trump said he was willing to work with Democrats to impose the cap, reviving a campaign pledge as Democrats prepare to take control of Congress in January 2027. Senator Elizabeth Warren welcomed the proposal, while Republican Senator Josh Hawley reiterated his support for rate-limiting legislation. The proposal aims to ease household borrowing costs at a time when credit-card debt and interest burdens remain elevated. According to the Federal Reserve Bank of New York data cited in recent reporting, the median credit-card rate was approximately 22.2% in August. The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau estimates that cardholders were assessed about $160 billion in interest charges in 2024, up from $105 billion in 2022. Researchers have suggested that a 10% ceiling could save consumers roughly $100 billion annually, although actual savings would depend on the legislation and lenders' responses. Trump first championed the idea during his 2024 presidential campaign and called for a one-year ceiling in January 2026. The proposal stalled amid banking-industry opposition and limited congressional support. Separately, Senators Bernie Sanders and Hawley introduced a bill in February 2025 proposing a five-year 10% cap. A proposed 10% cap on credit-card interest rates could pressure banks' earnings by reducing interest income from revolving balances without a corresponding decline in funding costs, servicing expenses or credit losses. Banks may respond by tightening underwriting standards, reducing credit limits, scaling back rewards or increasing permissible fees. These measures could constrain lending growth, customer spending and profitability. Citigroup faces meaningful exposure through its U.S. Consumer Cards business. As of Sept. 30, 2026, C had $177.9 billion in U.S. credit-card loans, comprising $150.3 billion in general-purpose cards and $27.6 billion in private-label cards. Including international operations, its consolidated consumer credit-card loans totaled approximately $192.5 billion. During the first nine months of 2026, Citigroup's U.S. Consumer Cards segment reported average loans of $176 billion, up 4% year over year. Net interest income increased 5% to $15.72 billion, while total revenues rose 2% to $13.94 billion. However, segment net income declined 4% to $2.44 billion, reflecting elevated operating expenses and credit costs. Card rewards and partner payments totaled $10.15 billion, underscoring the segment's substantial customer engagement costs. A rate cap could undermine further growth by squeezing lending margins and pressuring C's efforts to improve profitability and returns. JPMorgan has a larger credit-card portfolio in absolute terms. As of Sept. 30, 2026, Card Services loans totaled $252.7 billion, up 7% year over year. During the first nine months of 2026, average Card Services loans increased 7% to $244.3 billion. Card Services and Auto revenues rose 14% to $23.80 billion, while credit-card provisions for credit losses totaled $6 billion. Card Services' net charge-offs reached $5.90 billion, with a net charge-off rate of 3.23%. JPM reported company-wide net income of $53 billion in the first nine months of 2026, up 20% year over year from $44 billion. Credit-card lending remains an important contributor to its profitability, given the higher yields earned on revolving balances relative to many other lending products. An interest-rate ceiling could constrain card-related revenues and profitability despite continued loan growth. However, its diversified operations across investment banking, markets, asset management and consumer banking provide additional earnings support. Capital One appears particularly vulnerable because of its greater concentration in credit-card lending. As of Sept. 30, 2026, its credit-card loans totaled $276.4 billion, representing nearly 60% of its $462.5 billion total loan portfolio. Domestic credit-card loans accounted for approximately $260.3 billion. Capital One's net interest margin stood at 8.10% in the first nine months of 2026, highlighting the importance of interest earnings to its business model. Its Credit Card business generated net interest income of $28.11 billion and net income of $7.14 billion during the first nine months of 2026. The segment's significant contribution to overall profitability underscores the company's sensitivity to a potential mandatory reduction in credit-card borrowing rates. A 10% cap could significantly compress COF's interest income from revolving balances, limiting its ability to offset funding costs and credit losses. The company's expanded card portfolio following the Discover acquisition further increased its exposure to changes in credit-card pricing regulations. Although Capital One could respond through tighter underwriting, reduced rewards and other cost controls, such actions may affect customer acquisition, spending volumes and long-term growth. For now, the proposal represents an emerging downside risk rather than immediate earnings reset. Capital One appears the most exposed due to its substantial reliance on credit-card lending, while Citigroup faces risks to its ongoing profitability recovery. JPMorgan's diversified earnings base offers comparatively greater resilience, although its sizeable card portfolio remains vulnerable. Overall, all three stocks could face pressure if lawmakers move closer to implementing a binding interest-rate ceiling. title: USD.AI Appoints Affirm and J.P. Morgan Veterans to Lead Capital Markets and Originations - PR Newswire
content: Tony Giacin joins as Head of Capital Markets and Hani Abdul Baki as Head of Originations as USD.AI strengthens its institutional capital-markets capabilities. NEW YORK, Nov. 23, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- USD.AI, the platform financing the Compute Middle Market, today announced two senior appointments. Tony Giacin, formerly Director of Capital Markets at Affirm, joins as Head of Capital Markets. Hani Abdul Baki, formerly an Executive Director in Debt Capital Markets at J.P. Morgan, joins as Head of Originations. The hires add institutional depth across both sides of USD.AI's business: originating GPU loans, and building capital partnerships with private credit funds, banks and other institutional investors to finance the next phase of AI infrastructure. The appointments come as USD.AI moves toward its stated goal of issuing an asset-backed securitization collateralized solely by GPU financing. This would establish GPU loans as a standalone ABS sector, much as auto, credit card, student loan and mortgage receivables became single-sector asset classes before it. Giacin brings more than 12 years of securitization and debt capital markets experience. At Affirm, he spent four years in capital markets, most recently as Director, where he helped lead U.S. and international debt capital markets, asset-backed securitizations, loan sales and syndications, and investor relationships for one of fintech's most active ABS issuers. Before Affirm, he spent eight and a half years at Morgan Stanley as a Vice President in Fixed Income Sales & Trading, covering securitized products and corporate credit. At USD.AI, Giacin will lead the company's capital markets strategy, including its ABS program, forward-flow and loan sale partnerships, and relationships with institutional investors through the GPU Loans Exchange (GLX). "It has been proven that new financial asset classes and new collateral can access the securitization markets when the data and the structure are there. GPU loans have both: short duration, hard collateral and performance that can be underwritten at the pool level. Demand for compute financing is growing faster than the traditional lending market can keep up with, and the capital markets will need a dedicated product to meet it. I joined USD.AI to help the team continue to build that market." — Tony Giacin, Head of Capital Markets, USD.AI Abdul Baki joins USD.AI after more than a decade in Debt Capital Markets at J.P. Morgan in New York, most recently as Executive Director covering digital infrastructure and real estate. He brings deep experience structuring and raising financing for physical infrastructure, the same discipline that now applies to the GPUs, servers and facilities behind AI. As Head of Originations, Abdul Baki will lead origination and borrower relationships across the Compute Middle Market, the segment of GPU financings between $25 million and $500 million that sits between hyperscaler balance sheets and small equipment loans. "Data centers became an institutional asset class because banks set the underwriting standards and did the first deals, and that track record brought in the broader capital markets. Compute is on the same path, only faster. But banks are largely absent from the middle market, so someone else has to set the standards and build the track record. That's what USD.AI is doing, with capital that can scale as operators grow." — Hani Abdul Baki, Head of Originations, USD.AI Building institutional infrastructure for AI credit Together, the appointments reflect USD.AI's commitment to institutionalizing GPU credit: bringing the underwriting rigor, reporting standards and capital markets execution that institutional investors expect from established asset classes to a market that until now has been financed largely on a bilateral, deal-by-deal basis. "For GPU financing to become a real asset class, it needs the same people and processes that built the asset classes institutional investors already trust. With both Tony and Hani on board, we have the team to originate at institutional quality and to take that paper to the capital markets, starting with the first GPU-only ABS." — David Choi, CEO, USD.AI USD.AI is AI infrastructure financing for the Compute Middle Market, the GPU cloud operators between startups and hyperscalers. Operators finance new or deployed GPUs through USD.AI, and institutional capital holds the resulting GPU-backed loans through the GPU Loan Exchange (GLX), an institutional marketplace connecting that capital with qualified GPU financings. Every financing is structured the same way: a bankruptcy-remote special-purpose vehicle holds the GPUs, offtake contracts and revenue accounts, and capital is held in escrow until the servers are installed, burned in and independently verified. Compute IQ, USD.AI's agentic underwriting system, scores every deal against published underwriting standards. Borrowers get speed and certainty of execution. Lenders get secured exposure to income-producing compute. For more information, visit https://usd.ai.
